episodes.lead: The Houston Emancipation Day shooting took place before daylight on June 20, 1882, at the grounds where Black residents of Houston, Texas, were celebrating emancipation. Charles F. Witham, a white printer, was shot dead, Deputy Marshal Wm. Glass was wounded, and a Black man was killed and two Black people wounded by what the dispatches called stray shots. Several Black men were arrested, and three were later charged with Witham's murder.

episodes.title: Lynching of Epifanio near Smithville, Arizona
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Epifanio was the hanging of a Mexican prisoner by about thirty masked men near Smithville, Arizona Territory, in late June 1882. The men stopped a deputy sheriff and a district attorney who were taking him from Fort Thomas, seized him and hanged him. The wire report, which attributed the hanging to Mormons, ran in papers from Seattle to Pennsylvania.

episodes.title: Epes fire and expulsion of 1882
episodes.lead: The Epes fire and expulsion of 1882 was a clash in Epes, Sumter County, Alabama, on June 3, 1882, in which white men drove a crowd of Black men out of town and the town was burned that night. Seven stores burned, four Black men accused of setting the fire were arrested at Tuscaloosa, and papers reported fears that they would be lynched. The story ran widely in the white press as a case of "negro incendiaries" and "negro rioters."

episodes.title: Elm Bottom lynching report (1882)
episodes.lead: The Elm Bottom lynching report of 1882 was a widely circulated account that the bodies of four men, two hanged and two shot, had been found in the Elm bottom of Denton County, Texas, on the morning of June 22, 1882. Wire dispatches from Dallas presented the deaths as a lynching of cowboys or cattle thieves, and the story ran in papers from California to New Hampshire. The Dallas Daily Herald, the nearest paper in the coverage, doubted the rumor from the start and the next day called it a hoax.

episodes.title: Lynching of four rustlers near Mesilla
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of four rustlers near Mesilla was the killing, in New Mexico Territory in June 1882, of four unnamed men accused of robbing a store, who were overtaken by a posse and strangled. A Las Vegas dispatch described the dead as Americans from a gang of Arizona cowboys and the posse as Mexican, and said the men "richly deserved their fate." The story spread through the national telegraph columns within days but is known only from that single dispatch.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Beckett
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Beckett took place at Aberdeen, Monroe County, Mississippi, early on the morning of June 2, 1882, when a crowd took Beckett, a Black man, from the county jail and hanged him. He had been accused of attempting to outrage a girl of about seven years old. The case reached papers across the country ten days later through a St. Louis Post-Dispatch wire that misdated it to June 11, and was paired in news digests with lynchings at Rock Hill, South Carolina, and Lawrence, Kansas.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Ellis
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Ellis took place in the early hours of June 3, 1882, when masked men took him from the jail at Catlettsburg, Kentucky, and hanged him to a sycamore tree at Ashland. Ellis had been convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to life imprisonment the day before, on an indictment for the killing of three children at Ashland the previous December, after testifying against two co-defendants. The case was carried by wire across the country and drew editorials both excusing and condemning the mob.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Washington (New Mexico, 1882)
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Washington was the hanging by a mob of a Black man from Lincoln, New Mexico Territory, reported in June 1882. The only account found connects his death to his having eloped with a Mexican girl, and gives no date, place or names of the mob.

episodes.title: Lynching of Gus Mentzel and C. D. R. Bradley
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Gus Mentzel and C. D. R. Bradley took place in Raton, New Mexico Territory, in late June 1882, when citizens hanged the gambler Mentzel and then his partner Bradley. Mentzel was seized immediately after he was reported to have shot three men dead and wounded several others, including two deputy sheriffs, while resisting arrest. The story ran as a telegraph item in papers from New York to California, framed as a tale of a murderous gambler punished by an enraged town.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Huddleston
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Huddleston took place in Winchester, Franklin County, Tennessee, on the night of Sunday, June 18, 1882, when a crowd of men seized Huddleston, a young Black man, from guards in a room of the courthouse and hanged him from a tree in the courthouse yard. He had been accused of raping Mrs. Matt Vaughan, a white widow of the town, the night before. A coroner's jury found that he died by hanging "by the hands of unknown parties," and the story ran as a brief wire item in papers from Virginia to Utah.

episodes.title: Brooksville courthouse shooting
episodes.lead: The Brooksville courthouse shooting was a clash at the Hernando County courthouse in Brooksville, Florida, on the afternoon of June 29, 1882, in which white townspeople shot and killed three Black brothers, Henry, Jim and Rube Turner. Several other Black men were wounded and two or more white men were slightly hurt. Carried nationally from Jacksonville under headlines such as "Conflict of Races" and "A War of Races," the story was told entirely from the white side and blamed the Turners for the fight.

episodes.title: Lynching of Peter Vinegar, George Robertson and Isaac King
episodes.lead: The lynching of Peter Vinegar, George Robertson and Isaac King took place at Lawrence, Kansas, early on June 10, 1882, when masked men took the three Black prisoners from the Douglas County jail and hanged them from the Kansas river bridge. The men were charged with robbing and killing David Bausman, an Ohio farmer, and were reported to have confessed at a preliminary examination the day before. The case drew national wire coverage, a protest meeting by Black residents, and condemnation from Kansas papers.

episodes.title: Killing of Griffin Ingram
episodes.lead: The killing of Griffin Ingram was the shooting of a Black man by a member of a constable's posse on the Ponchatolowa in St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana, on June 21, 1882. Ingram was wanted on a warrant from Livingston parish, accused of murdering his young son, and the local paper reported that he was shot while resisting arrest. An inquest was held on his body, and the parish later paid its costs.

episodes.title: Lynching of James McHan
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of James McHan took place at Pecos, New Mexico Territory, about thirty miles south of Las Vegas, on the night of June 8, 1882, when a mob hanged a young railroad section hand accused of shooting a co-worker. McHan had fled after the killing of John Graves, was captured by about forty men and put under guard, and was then taken from his guards and hanged to a bridge in the station yard. A brief wire report of the case ran in papers from Washington to Nevada in the following two weeks.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Mitchell
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jim Mitchell took place on the night of June 14, 1882, at Mount Sterling, Kentucky, where armed men took Mitchell, a Black man, from the jail and hanged him from a railroad trestle. Mitchell had been jailed that day, accused of assaulting the wife of a local farmer. The Louisville dispatch that carried the story across the country said the whole community approved of the lynching.

episodes.title: Sale of John Hanson
episodes.lead: The sale of John Hanson was the public auction of a Black man into a year's servitude at the courthouse door in Louisville, Kentucky, on June 14, 1882, as punishment for vagrancy. A city scavenger bought him for two dollars. Papers across the country reported it as a return of slavery, the first such sale in the city since before the Civil War.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Johnson
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Johnson was the hanging of a 17-year-old Black youth by a crowd at Rock Hill, South Carolina, early on the morning of June 12, 1882. Johnson had been accused of assaulting Alice McDowell, a white girl, the day before, and was taken from a guard and hanged from a tree on Main Street. A coroner's jury found that he was hanged by persons unknown, and a Charleston wire carried the news to papers across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Tibbetts
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Tibbetts took place at Perham, Otter Tail County, Minnesota, in the early morning of June 9, 1882, when men broke into the jail and hanged the boy, reported as fifteen years old, from a telegraph pole. Tibbetts was accused of murdering a surveyor and his young companion north of the town. Papers across the country carried the case, and editors later used it to discuss crime among boys and the influence of dime novels.

episodes.title: Brighton train attack on Joliet strikebreakers
episodes.lead: The Brighton train attack was an assault by about fifty striking iron workers on non-union laborers of the Joliet Iron and Steel Company aboard a Chicago & Alton train at Brighton, Chicago, on the evening of June 1, 1882. Most of those dragged out and beaten were Black workers, and a stray shot wounded Judge N. J. Pillsbury of the Illinois appellate court, a passenger. No one was reported killed, several men were arrested, and the story ran nationally within coverage of the iron strike.

episodes.title: Lynching of Milan Howard
episodes.lead: The lynching of Milan Howard took place at the bridge over Bonfouca, in St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana, in June 1882, when about sixty men took Howard, a Black man accused of rape, from a constable and hanged him from the bridge. The parish paper approved the killing, and the parish later paid for his burial as a man "hung by unknown parties." Outside Louisiana the hanging circulated mainly as a joke item claiming that Oscar Wilde had watched it from a train.

episodes.title: Lynching of Morgan Hamilton
episodes.lead: The lynching of Morgan Hamilton was the shooting of a Black farm worker by a party of men carrying an arrest warrant in a field near Booneville, Mississippi, on the morning of Saturday, June 17, 1882. Hamilton had been accused of the murder of Miss Serena Benton and released by the inquest jury; the eight or ten men who went to re-arrest him shot him as he ran, and the sheriff set out after them. A Mississippi correspondent called the killing an outrage committed "on mere suspicion," while wire copy carried it across the country as the shooting of an accused murderer.

episodes.title: Lynching of Nathan Laird
episodes.lead: The lynching of Nathan Laird was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that took him from the jail at Sardis, Mississippi, early on the morning of June 21, 1882. Laird, named 'Nathan Lucid' in the wire report and 'Frank Layard' in a Memphis paper, was awaiting trial on a charge of raping or assaulting members of a white widow's household. The Sardis paper gave a detailed account of the jail raid, while papers across the country carried a one-sentence wire item.

episodes.title: Lynching of Navajo Frank
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Navajo Frank was the hanging of Francisco Tajoya, an Indian prisoner known as Navajo Frank, by a crowd of citizens at Las Vegas, New Mexico, in late June 1882. Accused of lassoing a man named R. H. Hutter and dragging him through the street, he was captured by a posse, then taken from the jail by force and hanged from a telegraph pole. A St. Louis telegraphic special carried the story nationally, often under headlines that cast the hanging as a fitting punishment.

episodes.title: Lewisville cabin shooting and rapes (1882)
episodes.lead: The Lewisville cabin shooting and rapes took place on the night of June 4, 1882, near Lewisville, Texas, when a group of armed men shot into the cabin of Perry Bolin, a Black man, forced their way in and raped two Black women. The accusation surfaced at a hearing on a separate complaint by two farmers whom the same men had shot at that night, and officers were reported to be pursuing the three accused.

episodes.title: Stabbing of Bernard McNally during the Baltimore G.A.R. parade
episodes.lead: The McNally stabbing in Baltimore took place on the evening of 21 June 1882, when boys threw stones at a parading Black division of the Grand Army of the Republic and a member of the column fatally stabbed Bernard McNally, a youth standing at the corner of Madison and Constitution streets. George H. Brightman, the Black vice-commander of Lincoln Post, was charged with murder after a coroner's jury named him, but he was acquitted in December 1882 when the state conceded its evidence was insufficient.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Herman Schmidt
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Herman Schmidt took place in Chico, California, on the night of June 24, 1882, when a crowd gathered after Schmidt, a saloon keeper, was accused of shooting his wife dead. Officers misled the crowd and Schmidt was not harmed; he was tried, convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to hang within two weeks. The papers gave more attention to the speed of the court proceedings than to the crowd, and none of them stated Schmidt's race.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Herman Schmidt
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Herman Schmidt followed the shooting of a saloon keeper's wife in Chico, California, on the night of June 24, 1882. Wire dispatches said a crowd had gathered and that he would probably be lynched before morning, but he was instead tried at Oroville, convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to hang. Later reports drew notice to how quickly the court had disposed of the case.

episodes.title: Third Ward polling-place assaults, Wilmington, 1882
episodes.lead: The Third Ward polling-place assaults took place on 3 June 1882 at the Third Ward polls in Wilmington, Delaware, during a municipal election, when a crowd of Democrats drove colored voters from the polls and beat two men who vouched for them. Mr. Burchall was badly beaten and Edmund Mitchell nearly killed, according to the Republican Daily Republican, the only paper found to report the assaults.

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas Wall and Trinidad Charlie
episodes.lead: The lynching of Thomas Wall and Trinidad Charlie took place at Rico, Colorado, at about 2 a.m. on June 16, 1882, when a party entered the town jail, took out the two prisoners and hanged them in a small cabin opposite. The men were accused of killing Rico's marshal, and the wire report of their deaths ran in papers across the country under headings such as "Two Murderers Lynched in Colorado." Only one syndicated brief described them as "two colored desperadoes."

episodes.title: Burning of Thomas J. Archer's farm, Cardington, Ohio
episodes.lead: The burning of Thomas J. Archer's farm took place near Cardington, Ohio, on the night of June 5, 1882, when a mob burned the house, barn and farm buildings of Archer, a Black man, while he was held in jail for shooting three people. The sheriff kept Archer from a crowd that had threatened to lynch him, and the story circulated in Ohio and beyond because the quarrel was said to have begun with neighbors refusing to call him "Mister Archer."

episodes.title: Lynching of three men at Butlerville, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The lynching of three men at Butlerville, Arkansas, took place on the night of Sunday, June 4, 1882, when a mob took three Black men from officers at Butlerville, in Lonoke County, and hanged them to a tree. The men, who were not named, were accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old girl, Annie Bridges, although an earlier report had called the story untrue. A Little Rock dispatch of June 5 carried the news to papers across the country, many under headlines presenting the hanging as just punishment.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Tibbetts
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Tibbetts took place at Perham, Otter Tail County, Minnesota, at about one o'clock on the morning of June 9, 1882, when twenty men broke into the jail and hanged him from a ladder set against a telegraph pole. Tibbetts, a youth whose age the papers gave as anywhere from 12 to 17, was accused of murdering two men near the Red Eye about ten days earlier. Papers across the country carried it as the story of a "boy murderer" corrupted by dime novels, and several editorials used it to condemn lynching.

episodes.title: Killing of William Broder
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of William Broder was the shooting of a saloon keeper by vigilantes at Park Station, Montana Territory, on the night of June 15, 1882. Broder was called to the door of his saloon and shot dead, the vigilantes' stated reason being that his place was a resort for thieves. The news reached the wider press only as a one-sentence wire item, which Pacific coast dailies and Midwestern weeklies reprinted over the following two weeks.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Tolly
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Tolly was the hanging of a young Black man by a mob at Elizabethtown, Illinois, on the evening of Monday, June 26, 1882. He was accused of trying to break into the house of Mrs. Howe, but she could not identify him, and a witness said he had been elsewhere. Papers across the country carried the story because the man hanged was believed to be innocent, under headlines such as "Hanged the Wrong Man."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Alfred Ross
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Alfred Ross took place in Memphis, Tennessee, on the evening of July 24, 1882, when a crowd tried to hang Ross, a Black steamboat roustabout, as officers brought him out to be identified. Ross had been accused that morning of striking an aged Italian grocer, John Genochio, with a rock. Bystanders held the crowd back, and Ross was later bound over to the Criminal Court.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Anderson Bunch
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Anderson Bunch was the reported hanging, in July 1882, of a man near Paoli, Indiana, who was accused of helping the accused murderer of Martin H. Archer to escape. Wire dispatches from New Albany, which called him Bundy, said a mob hanged him at night and threw his body into Lost River, and the story ran in papers from Maine to Arizona. The local Paoli News, however, reported only that he had disappeared and that foul play was suspected.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Huff
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Charles Huff took place on the morning of July 12, 1882, when a mob captured Huff, described as a young cattle thief, and hanged him to a tree five miles from Denver, Colorado. Police attacked the mob, and Huff was cut down and resuscitated. None of the reports give Huff's race.

episodes.title: Lynching of David Cook
episodes.lead: The lynching of David Cook was the killing of a young Black man by masked men in northern Kershaw County, South Carolina, in July 1882, after he was taken from officers who were conveying him to Camden. Cook, accused of attempted rape, was seized on Saturday, July 15, and his body was found two days later hanging from a tree. A Charleston wire report carried the story to papers across the country, most of them repeating its claim that he had confessed.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dennis McLellan
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dennis McLellan took place in Kemper County, Mississippi, on July 15, 1882, when armed men took the Black youth from a deputy's guard on the road to the county jail at DeKalb and, it was supposed, hanged him. He had been accused of entering the bedroom of a Kemper County man's ten-year-old daughter the night before. The only source, the Meridian Observer, did not confirm his death but endorsed the lynching, and papers that reprinted it praised the act.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed Sayles
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ed Sayles was the hanging of a Black youth by a masked band at Iredell, Texas, on the night of July 6, 1882. Sayles, accused that morning of raping a farmer's wife, was taken from his guards and hanged from a pecan tree near the depot. The wire carried the story across the country, often under headlines that approved the killing.

episodes.title: Castration of Eli McKnight
episodes.lead: The castration of Eli McKnight was a mob attack on a Black man near Gurdon station, Arkansas, on the night of Tuesday, July 25, 1882. Accused of trying to rape Miss Baker, a young woman of the neighborhood, he was captured that evening and castrated by a mob, and a Little Rock Gazette dispatch reported that he would recover. The story spread by wire to papers from Tennessee to Pennsylvania and Washington, D.C., often under headlines that treated the mutilation as a deserved punishment.

episodes.title: Killing of Tom Jones at Louisville, Mississippi
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of Tom Jones at Louisville, Mississippi, was the fatal shooting of Tom Jones by F. L. Jones, a local photographer, in front of a Louisville store in early July 1882. Wire dispatches reported that a large crowd threatened to lynch the killer as he was taken to jail, and that a strong guard prevented it. He was convicted of murder at the next circuit court and sentenced to hang, then granted an appeal on the day set for his execution.

episodes.title: Homestead drug store siege (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Homestead drug store siege was a threatened lynching at Homestead, Pennsylvania, on the evening of July 16, 1882, when a crowd surrounded a drug store where a man named Fowley had taken refuge after shooting a man named Critchlow. The crowd demanded Fowley and threatened to break in, but it dispersed without violence and he was jailed in Pittsburgh the next morning. Later reports tied the quarrel to a strike at the Bessemer Steel Company's mill, and none of the reports gives the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Killing of Frank Clinton
episodes.lead: The killing of Frank Clinton was the shooting of a Black man at Marion, Mississippi, by unknown parties, reported in July 1882. Clinton, who was said to have had two children with a white woman, was "riddled with forty-eight bullets," and the only report found gives no motive, names no attackers and records no arrests.

episodes.title: Rock Creek assault on Eunice Martin
episodes.lead: The Rock Creek assault on Eunice Martin was a reported attack on an eight-year-old Black girl by three white youths near the Twentieth street bridge over Rock Creek in Washington, D.C., in mid-July 1882. The Evening Critic and an Associated Press dispatch described it as a sexual assault that left the child in critical condition, but a police report days later said she had only been driven from a spring and stoned. Several boys were arrested and all were discharged.

episodes.title: Las Vegas jail attack of 1882
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Las Vegas jail attack of 1882 was an attempt by a crowd of about 100 to 150 men to break into the jail at Las Vegas, New Mexico Territory, in the early hours of July 12, 1882, and hang the prisoner H. C. Brown, accused of killing the butcher Frank Mayer. Sheriff Romero's guard fired on the crowd from the jail and drove it off, and a fourteen-year-old in the crowd, Eddie Brown, later died of his wounds. Wire reports carried the repulse across the country as the work of a mob of Germans avenging one of their own.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Caldwell
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Caldwell took place shortly after midnight on July 30, 1882, when a disguised mob took Caldwell, a Black man held on a charge of assaulting an elderly white woman, from the Iron County jail at Ironton, Missouri, and hanged and shot him from the Iron Mountain Railroad bridge. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of a mob whose members were unknown to it. The local weekly endorsed the killing, while St. Louis wire reports carried it to papers across the country under headlines such as 'A Ravisher Lynched.'

episodes.title: Musick's Ferry mob attack on Franz Suppenbach
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Musick's Ferry mob attack on Franz Suppenbach took place in mid-July 1882 at Musick's Ferry, St. Louis County, Missouri, when a crowd of Black men went at night to the house of a German laborer who was living with a Black woman. The German fired a musket into the crowd, and first wire reports said he had killed a preacher and was then drowned or hanged by the mob. Corrections a week later said that no one had died and that the man, named in them as Franz Suppenbach, had walked to St. Louis with the woman.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Green
episodes.lead: The killing of Henry Green was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Deputy Sheriff T. G. Martin at Kyle, Texas, on Sunday, July 30, 1882, while Martin was trying to arrest him on a warrant. Green died the next day in the jail at San Marcos, and a coroner's jury found that he died of a shot fired by Martin, who was bound over to the district court.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of James Hawks
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of James Hawks took place in Syracuse, New York, on the afternoon of July 9, 1882, when a crowd pursued Hawks, a laborer accused of stabbing a woman to death, with cries of "Lynch him!" and surrounded the police station where he was held. No attack on the station was reported, and Hawks was convicted of second-degree murder that December and sent to prison for life. Most papers treated the case as a wife murder, and only one widely reprinted dispatch mentioned the crowd.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joe Harrison
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Joe Harrison took place at Big Timber, Gallatin County, Montana Territory, about 3 a.m. on July 7, 1882, when twenty to thirty men overpowered his guards and hanged and shot him. Harrison was being held for a hearing on the charge of shooting Miss Flora Cutler, the Sweet Grass school teacher, who survived paralyzed. Montana papers reported the killing with approval, and no paper in the coverage gives Harrison's race.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Davis
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John Davis took place in Stamford in late July or early August 1882, when friends of women and girls he was accused of trying to assault lay in wait to lynch him. Officers arrested Davis and sent him to jail first, and a Connecticut weekly credited the arrest with preventing his death.

episodes.title: Fargo manhunt for Knudson (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Fargo manhunt for Knudson was a search by townspeople of Fargo, Dakota Territory, on the night of July 5, 1882, for a Norwegian man they meant to lynch as the killer of Policeman Fred D. Alderman. Knudson was not found, and by morning a woman, Mrs. Martin Bunkle, had confessed that she shot the officer after taking him for a tramp. Papers outside Dakota noted that the crowd would have hanged an innocent man.

episodes.title: Lynching of Mack Taylor
episodes.lead: The lynching of Mack Taylor was the killing of a 14-year-old Black boy in Webster Parish, Louisiana, in June 1882 by three white men who seized him in Arkansas, brought him back, tied him to a tree and shot him. A coroner's jury named Edward McDonald, the father of a white boy Taylor was accused of beating, and two men who helped him. A Shreveport dispatch describing the remains as picked bare by vultures ran in papers across the country under headlines of revenge and butchery.

episodes.title: Lynching of Martin Becket
episodes.lead: The lynching of Martin Becket was the killing of a Black man taken from the jail at Hampton Courthouse, South Carolina, on the night of Tuesday, July 25, 1882. Becket had been jailed on an accusation of assaulting a white girl about twelve years old, and a crowd reported at some three hundred took him out and lynched him. A placard reading "Our women must be protected" was left with his body, and its words became the headline under which the story ran across the country.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Mexican Frank at Tascosa, Texas
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Mexican Frank was the reported killing, in late July 1882, of a man called Mexican Frank or Marion Frank by a posse near Tascosa, Oldham County, Texas, after he was accused of shooting Deputy Sheriff Henry McCullough. The news spread nationally as a brief wire item, but every version described the lynching as reported rather than confirmed. Two weeks later a Texas Ranger captain reported that the deputy's killer had been arrested, leaving the outcome in doubt.

episodes.title: Killing of George Bentley
episodes.lead: The killing of George Bentley was the fatal shooting of a Black miner from Marietta, Georgia, by a white man named Sam Hunt at the copper mines in Haralson County, Georgia, in early July 1882. Hunt fled after the shooting, and two other miners were jailed over an earlier roadside assault. An Atlanta wire report presented Hunt as a constable who killed a miner resisting arrest, while Bentley's hometown paper described him only as a white man who returned with friends after losing a fight.

episodes.title: Killing of Bill Mulcahy, Jack Kingsbury and Nevada Jim
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of Bill Mulcahy, Jack Kingsbury and Nevada Jim took place in Sonora, Mexico, in July 1882, when a party of armed men from Calabasas, Arizona Territory, pursued the three across the border and killed them. Mulcahy and Kingsbury were shot dead in a gunfight, and Nevada Jim, wounded and held while a rope was found to hang him, shot one of his captors and then himself. Wire services carried the story nationally as the work of "Arizona vigilantes", with a closing note that local citizens approved.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Noah Parks
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Noah Parks was the hanging of a Black preacher by a mob in Winston County, Mississippi, in the summer of 1882. Accused of stealing corn, Parks was taken from his house at night and hanged to a tree, but friends cut him down and revived him. The story ran nationally as a brief wire item, and at least one Western paper treated it as a completed lynching and endorsed it.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Otho Gilmore
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Otho Gilmore took place at Martin's Ferry, Belmont County, Ohio, on the night of July 26, 1882, when a large crowd talked of hanging Gilmore, a Black prisoner, after he cut a police officer and a citizen with a razor in the town lockup. A guard was placed at the jail, and the crowd broke up once the wounded men were expected to live. Gilmore, who had been shot twice by the officer, recovered and was sentenced in December to four years in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Tarring and feathering of Paul Ellis
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The tarring and feathering of Paul Ellis took place on the night of July 6, 1882, in Shrewsbury, Vermont, when fifteen to twenty-five men put a rope around his neck at a tree, threatened to hang him, and coated him with tar and feathers. The men accused Ellis of an attempted assault on a fourteen-year-old girl, a charge a justice soon dismissed for lack of evidence. Papers noted that a justice of the peace and wealthy farmers led the mob, and in October the participants pleaded guilty and paid $12.50 each.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Caldwell
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Caldwell took place early on July 30, 1882, when a masked mob took Caldwell, a Black man, from the Iron County jail at Ironton, Missouri, and hanged and shot him at a railroad bridge southeast of town. Caldwell had been bound over for trial on a charge of assaulting Mrs. Peck, a white woman of about sixty. The St. Louis wire spread the story nationally, some versions misplacing it at "Canton," while the local paper openly endorsed the killing.

episodes.title: Killing of Pedro Aguilar near Laredo (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of Pedro Aguilar near Laredo was the killing of a Mexican man by a crowd during a fight among Mexicans at a place reported as Fernando or Fernandez, near Laredo, in late July 1882. After another man, Pedro Gomez, was shot dead, Aguilar complained that he had not had fair play, and the crowd killed him too. The item circulated in northern papers only as a one-sentence wire brief within crime roundups.

episodes.title: Killing of a smallpox patient near Red Clay, Georgia
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of a smallpox patient near Red Clay, Georgia, took place in mid-July 1882, when railroad laborers shot an unnamed Black man who had been quarantined in an isolated cabin and then set the cabin on fire. Warrants were issued against several men, but the local paper reported no conclusive evidence of who took part. A one-line wire item carried the killing across the country, and a fuller Georgia account was later reprinted as 'Murder as a Cure for Small-Pox.'

episodes.title: Rockmart tunnel riot
episodes.lead: The Rockmart tunnel riot was a gunfight on July 15, 1882, at a railroad tunnel in Paulding County, Georgia, about seven miles from Rockmart, after a white man, John Hicks, tried without authority to disarm Black railroad hands. Hicks's party shot a Black worker named Tom Laws, who was reported dying and later dead, and the Black workers then killed Hicks. The papers treated it as a race riot, and it ended in the arrest of some thirty Black workers, four life sentences for murder and a death sentence for a man called the riot's leader.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Jim Brown and "Blind Jim" at Flagstaff
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Jim Brown and "Blind Jim" at Flagstaff was the hanging, announced in July 1882, of two men accused of shooting two residents of Flagstaff, then in Arizona Territory though wire reports placed it in New Mexico. Wire dispatches said the whole town had caught and hanged them, and the item entered a year-end chronology as "Two murderers lynched at Flagstaff, N. M." Weeks later, however, Blind Jim was arrested alive in Kansas, and he was acquitted of murder at Prescott that winter.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of W. H. Yeatts
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of W. H. Yeatts was an effort by a mounted, armed mob to take the condemned murderer Walter Hamilton Yeatts from the jail at Chatham, Pittsylvania County, Virginia, and hang him early on Saturday, July 29, 1882. The party, numbered at between sixty-five and a hundred men, dispersed without attacking the jail, and Yeatts was legally hanged at Chatham a week later. Yeatts was white, and the papers treated the episode as a sequel to a much-followed Virginia murder case.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Ritter
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Ritter took place in the early hours of July 12, 1882, when a masked mob took Ritter, a Black man, from the jail at Henderson, Kentucky, and hanged him on a tree about a mile outside the town. Ritter had been charged with the rape and murder of Helen Brewster, a Black girl from the county. The papers treated the case as notable because the mob was reported to include both Black and white men, and the Henderson Reporter called it the first lynching in the county's history.

episodes.title: Cowtown attack on the Washington poundmen
episodes.lead: The Cowtown attack on the Washington poundmen was an assault by a crowd of residents of the 'Cowtown' neighborhood of Washington, D.C., on the city poundmaster and his men on the morning of August 19, 1882, in which a Black poundman, Albert Fortune, was struck on the head with a stone. During the fray a resident, John Keefe, called for a gun to 'kill the niggers', and four residents were fined or forfeited collateral in Police Court.

episodes.title: Oatmanville shooting of Augustin Agirer
episodes.lead: The Oatmanville shooting of Augustin Agirer was an attack on August 8, 1882, near Oatmanville in Travis County, Texas, in which two young white men shot Agirer and another Mexican, Redel, on the road home from a justice court where Agirer had won a complaint against their friend. Early reports said Agirer was killed, but an Austin dispatch the next day said both men were still alive and expected to die, and the shooters escaped arrest with help from friends.

episodes.title: Killing of Ben Harris
episodes.lead: The killing of Ben Harris took place on August 26, 1882, near Visalia, Tulare County, California, when a Black man accused of murdering his stepdaughter and wounding his wife was shot dead by a pursuer, John Dice, while trying to escape. Harris had been hunted for four days by a party of twenty or thirty men, and wire reports of both the killings and his death ran in papers across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bishop Emberton and Richard Speakman
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bishop Emberton and Richard Speakman took place in Kentucky on or about August 1, 1882, when a mob took the two white men from a guard moving them from the Tompkinsville jail to Glasgow and killed them about thirteen miles from Glasgow. The men had been charged with assaulting Mrs. J. B. Garrett near Tompkinsville in Monroe County. The killing was carried by wire across the country, and several papers headlined it as deserved or justified.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Young and Charlie Griffin
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bob Young and Charlie Griffin was the hanging of two Black prisoners by a mob of about forty men near La Fayette, Chambers County, Alabama, in August 1882. The two had been convicted of murdering a white man named McCann, but their conviction had been reversed on appeal and a new trial ordered when the mob took them from the jail. Wire reports carried the killing to papers across the country, several of which noted that the men protested their innocence to the end.

episodes.title: Killing of Booth near Satartia
episodes.lead: The killing of Booth was the fatal shooting of a Black man named Booth near Satartia, Yazoo County, Mississippi, on Saturday, August 12, 1882, by two white men after he refused to let them ride in his wagon. Both men escaped, and a Jackson dispatch on the shooting ran in papers across the country, several of which headlined it as murder.

episodes.title: Killing of the Campbell brothers
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of the Campbell brothers was the mob killing of Bud and Reilly Campbell, two men described as 'desperadoes', at their house in Caldwell County, Kentucky, in August 1882. A mob of 25 to 40 men besieged the house at night, set it on fire and killed both brothers, losing one of its own members in the gunfire. Wire reports carried the story nationally within a day, and in October it was retold at length as the prelude to the lynching of Mary Sullivan.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Savage and Howard James
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Savage and Howard James was the shooting of two Black prisoners by a mob at the railroad depot in Madison, Florida, on the morning of August 25, 1882. The men, convicted of the 1881 killing of Frank Patterson but granted a new trial, were being taken under a sheriff's guard to Jasper for retrial when armed men stopped the train and shot them. Governor William D. Bloxham offered a $5,000 reward, but a coroner's jury found that they died at the hands of parties unknown, and no one was reported tried.

episodes.title: Phoenix cowboy fight and attempted lynching
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Phoenix cowboy fight and attempted lynching took place on August 2, 1882, in Phoenix, Arizona Territory, when city marshal Henry Garfias and a posse fought three mounted men described as cowboys, killing one, and a crowd then tried to hang the captured survivors on the way to jail. Officers with a posse rescued the prisoners, who were later discharged by a justice court and fined $100. The wire story ran in papers from Savannah to Nevada as a near escape from lynching, while the local Phoenix Herald praised the marshal and warned that future captives might not reach jail.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dan Blakeney
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dan Blakeney was the hanging of a Black farm hand near Lancaster, South Carolina, on August 8, 1882, by a body of men who took him from constables escorting him to jail. He had been accused of attempting to assault the twelve-year-old daughter of his employer the night before. The Charleston News and Courier's Lancaster correspondent, who saw the body, endorsed the killing, and a short wire version of his report ran in papers across the country.

episodes.title: Killing of Ed McElroy
episodes.lead: The killing of Ed McElroy took place at Frankfort, Kentucky, on the afternoon of August 7, 1882, a local election day, when a crowd at the polls shot dead McElroy, a Black man, after he fired a gun while officers tried to arrest him. The shot from McElroy's gun seriously wounded a man named Bud, or Sanford, Egbert. Telegraph dispatches carried the story across the country within days, most under headlines that cast McElroy as a "desperado" or "murderer."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Liberty Kennedy
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Liberty Kennedy took place in Hannibal, Missouri, on August 22, 1882, when a crowd of white citizens chased down Kennedy, a young Black man accused with Edward Murphy of assaulting a white girl, and relatives of the girl tried to kill him. The attempt failed and both men were jailed, but the wire dispatch that carried the story across the country predicted they would be lynched at their examination.

episodes.title: Police killing of Frank Hagan
episodes.lead: The police killing of Frank Hagan took place near Leavenworth, Kansas, in early August 1882, when a policeman shot Hagan, a Black man, three times while trying to arrest him after a shooting at an emancipation celebration. Hagan died on August 4, and a coroner's inquest exculpated the officer, identified in a follow-up dispatch as Policeman Shepherd. The story ran as a short telegraphic item in papers from Memphis to Savannah, one of which headed it "A Negro Desperado Killed."

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Frank Lane
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Frank Lane was the reported seizure and killing by a mob of a man accused of stabbing two card players at Mountainburg, Arkansas, on the night of August 24, 1882. A wire dispatch from Alma said only that Lane was in a mob's hands and believed already lynched, and no report found confirms his fate. The dispatch nonetheless circulated nationally, and some roundups reported the lynching as fact.

episodes.title: Lynching at Deming, New Mexico (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching at Deming, New Mexico, was the hanging of an unnamed man by a mob of citizens on the evening of Sunday, August 27, 1882, hours after he was jailed for cutting the throat of a Frenchman. Taken from the jail, he was hanged from a telegraph pole by the railroad track and left there until late the next morning. The story ran as a short wire item from Washington to Montana, often under headlines that treated it as rough justice, and none of the reports gave the race of either man.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Lenhart
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Lenhart took place in August 1882 in and around Evansville, Indiana, after Lenhart, a German laborer, was arrested in the murder of saloon keeper Alexander Wieber, his wife and their young son. A vigilance committee was organized and men were reported gathering to lynch him, but the sheriff moved him to the jail at Boonville in Warrick County. In December 1882 Lenhart was discharged when the State attorney could not make a case, and a German-language paper cited the affair as proof that innocent men could fall victim to lynch law.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Porter
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Porter was the killing of a man by a mob in Lampasas County, Texas, on the night of August 2, 1882. About twenty-five men took Porter from a cattleman's camp and shot him to death because he was suspected of horse stealing. The killing was reported in a Lampasas letter to the Dallas Herald and then spread as a one-sentence wire item to papers in several states.

episodes.title: Mandan citizens' order to Ira Hall and John Trumbull to leave town
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Mandan citizens' order to Ira Hall and John Trumbull to leave town was a threat of lynching made on August 28, 1882, when a mass meeting in Mandan, Dakota Territory, sent a committee to tell the two men, accused in the killing of Jacob Book, to leave by noon the next day. Hall promised to go and Trumbull disappeared, and no report shows that either man was harmed. Territorial papers treated the meeting as the climax of local anger at a federal commissioner who had freed one of the accused.

episodes.title: Killing of Hugh Burns and threatened lynching of John J. Jater
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of Hugh Burns and threatened lynching of John J. Jater took place in Indianapolis, Indiana, on the night of August 28, 1882, when a Kentucky man named in the papers as Jater shot and killed Policeman Hugh Burns, who was trying to arrest him. Jater was caught and jailed, and a widely reprinted telegram said he had "narrowly escaped lynching." No report gave Jater's race or described the threat in racial terms.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Turner
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jack Turner took place at Butler, the county seat of Choctaw County, Alabama, on August 19, 1882, when a crowd took Turner, a Black Republican leader, from jail and hanged him on the vote of a mass meeting. He had been jailed with several other Black men on the charge of leading a plot to massacre the county's white population, a charge resting on papers said to have been found by two white men. Republican papers and Black Republicans called the plot an invention meant to intimidate Black voters, and the governor's office asked county officers for an investigation, which they answered with a defense of the hanging.

episodes.title: Eastman camp meeting riot
episodes.lead: The Eastman camp meeting riot took place on Sunday, August 6, 1882, at Eastman, Dodge County, Georgia, when the town marshal's party shot dead a Black prisoner fleeing arrest and a crowd of Black excursionists then killed a young white man, James Q. Harvard, whom they took for one of the officers. Two accounts add that armed white citizens then killed three Black men in a clash with the crowd. Twenty-two Black defendants were convicted of Harvard's murder, five were hanged together at Eastman in October, and the two officers were indicted for manslaughter.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Mullins
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Mullins was the shooting of a Black man by a crowd of about fifteen men at his sister's house on Topisaw, near Tyler's mill, Mississippi, on the night of August 10, 1882. Mullins had been accused of attempting an outrage on a white woman in Lawrence County, and the local paper reported his killing under the heading "The Perpetrator Summarily Dealt with."

episodes.title: Killing of John Wesley
episodes.lead: The killing of John Wesley was the shotgun murder of a well-to-do Black farmer at his home in southwestern Arkansas in the summer of 1882. Reports attributed the killing to young white men, and an attempt to arrest two suspects left a constable and two of his posse dead. Brothers named Coyle were later tried in Miller County circuit court, where the first defendant was acquitted and the charges against the others were dropped.

episodes.title: Killing of Primus Johnson
episodes.lead: The killing of Primus Johnson was the death of a Black man at Shell Mound, on the Tallahatchie River in Mississippi, in early August 1882, during a white posse's pursuit of a Black man accused of attacking a white planter. A telegraphic report said the posse captured Johnson and a mob shot him dead, while a Mississippi paper said he was killed trying to escape from officers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Juan Elverad
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Juan Elverad took place in Socorro, New Mexico Territory, in mid-August 1882, when a crowd took a man accused of raping an eight-year-old girl from the town jail and hanged him to a tree. A coroner's inquest found that he died 'at the hands of unknown parties,' and wire reports carried the hanging across the country under approving headlines.

episodes.title: Lynching of Curtis B. Hawley and L. V. Grimes
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Curtis B. Hawley and L. V. Grimes was the hanging of two white men by a crowd of citizens at Globe, Arizona Territory, on August 24, 1882, after they confessed to a Wells, Fargo & Co. robbery in which messenger Andy Hall and Dr. W. F. Vail were killed. The crowd spared a third man, Grimes's older brother Cicero, who was later sentenced to 21 years in prison. Wire reports carried the hanging nationally within a day, while Arizona papers printed long accounts of the crowd's orderly proceedings.

episodes.title: Lynching of Leonard Coker
episodes.lead: The lynching of Leonard Coker was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of whites and blacks near Cowles Station, Alabama, about 30 miles east of Montgomery, on August 25, 1882. Coker was accused of outraging and murdering a white woman, most often named as Catharine Haynes, and was hanged to a tree at the scene of the alleged crime after a search and a reported confession. An Associated Press dispatch from Montgomery carried the story to papers across the country, several of which presented the killing as deserved.

episodes.title: Killing of the McCoy brothers in Pike County, Kentucky
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of the McCoy brothers was the shooting of three McCoys by friends of a slain Hatfield in Pike County, Kentucky, after an election-day affray in August 1882. The brothers, under arrest for the killing, were taken from their guard by about fifty men, tied to a tree in the woods and shot. Papers across the country carried the story as a Kentucky family vendetta, and a later Kentucky report said no member of the mob had been arrested.

episodes.title: Taylorville jail mob of 1882
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Taylorville jail mob of 1882 was a series of attempts by crowds in Taylorville, Christian County, Illinois, to lynch Lee Pettis, John C. Montgomery and Emanuel Clementi, three men accused of assaulting schoolteacher Emma Bond. After threats against the jail in early July, a crowd of thousands took the prisoners from the jail about midnight on August 11-12 and hoisted Montgomery by the neck to force a confession, but returned all three to jail alive. Papers across the country followed the case, first presuming the men lynched and then printing detailed accounts of their pleas of innocence.

episodes.title: Lynching of P. A. Rymer
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of P. A. Rymer was the hanging of a U.S. Army soldier from Fort Lyon, Colorado, by a masked mob that took him from the jail at West Las Animas on the night of August 20, 1882. Rymer was accused of having stabbed a fellow soldier, William McGarvey, to death two nights earlier. Wire reports said the mob of forty or fifty men was supposed to be soldiers from the fort, and the story ran across the country under headlines such as "Lynched by Soldiers" and "Military Hanging."

episodes.title: Nettleton railroad laborers' expulsion
episodes.lead: The Nettleton railroad laborers' expulsion was the driving off of Black construction workers from a railroad line near Nettleton, Craighead County, Arkansas, in mid-August 1882 by armed men disguised as Ku Klux. The contractors and the railroad's president appealed to Governor T. J. Churchill, who ordered the county sheriff to protect the workers, and within a week the men were reported back at work. Papers across the country carried the story as a revival of the Ku Klux and a clash between white and Black laborers.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Riley Wiggins
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Riley Wiggins was an attempt in early August 1882 to lynch a Black hotel cook held in the jail at El Paso, Texas, after he killed two Mexicans who had shot him. Officials kept him safe, and the Dallas Daily Herald reported the case because Wiggins had been a well-known waiter at a Dallas hotel.

episodes.title: Lynching of Gibbon at Rock Creek, Wyoming
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Gibbon took place at Rock Creek, Albany County, Wyoming Territory, on the evening of August 21, 1882, when citizens hanged a hunter named Gibbon from a railroad box car hours after he was accused of shooting a store clerk, Robert Aiken. No one is reported to have been arrested for the hanging, and the Laramie dispatch on it ran widely under the heading "Lynch Law." None of the reports gives the race of Gibbon, Aiken or the men who hanged him.

episodes.title: Lynching of A. Brown (Sam Miller)
episodes.lead: The lynching of A. Brown (Sam Miller) was the hanging of a Black man by a party of men who took him from the jail at Newnan, Georgia, on the night of August 9, 1882. He had been accused of outraging a fifteen-year-old white girl in Campbell County and brought to Newnan for safe keeping. An Atlanta dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and several papers printed it under headings approving the killing.

episodes.title: Killing of Sandy Bynum
episodes.lead: The killing of Sandy Bynum was the fatal shooting of a Black Republican leader by Thomas G. Hewlett, a former U.S. deputy marshal, at a political barbecue at Ayer's Spring near Huntsville, Alabama, on August 5, 1882. Hewlett fled on horseback, was later tried for second-degree murder, and was acquitted. Telegraphed across the country, the killing became a talking point in the partisan press over political violence in the South.

episodes.title: Prineville lynching rumor of August 1882
episodes.lead: The Prineville lynching rumor of August 1882 was a report, carried to Albany, Oregon, by a traveler, that a mob at Prineville had lynched five young men from Linn County for stealing horses. Portland dispatches spread the story to California and Nevada papers, but within days the Associated Press agent at The Dalles reported that no lynching had taken place, and the Albany paper that first printed the rumor declared it ill-founded.

episodes.title: Lynching of Smith near Little Rock
episodes.lead: The lynching of Smith near Little Rock was the killing of a Black man known only as Smith by a disguised party in Arkansas on or about August 24, 1882. He was accused of attempting to outrage a white woman, and a wire dispatch reporting that he had been shot to death ran in papers across the country within days.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Sylvanus K. Makison
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Sylvanus K. Makison took place at Kewanee, Henry County, Illinois, between August 28 and August 31, 1882, when crowds of men tried to seize and hang the farm hand, who was jailed for the murder of Mrs. Maggie Copeland. Officers, citizens and the state's attorney held the crowds back with promises that the law would take its course, and Makison was removed alive to the jail at Cambridge. The case drew wide notice because it coincided with the Kewanee bank robbery and because Makison, after confessing, asked to be handed over to the mob.

episodes.title: Troy depot crowd incident
episodes.lead: The Troy depot crowd incident was a confrontation at the railway depot in Troy, Pennsylvania, about August 25, 1882, in which a crowd shouted threats at a Black man boarding a night train with a white woman. Told that the pair were eloping, the crowd cried "Hang the man," and the man left the train; no one was reported hurt.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Holmes
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Holmes took place on the night of Sunday, August 6, 1882, when a mob of about a hundred men surrounded the jail at Pomeroy, Ohio, to seize Holmes, a Black man charged with outraging a young white girl near Rutland. The men nearly broke through the jail walls before learning that Holmes had already been taken away and sent to Columbus for safekeeping. The case drew further notice when two alleged leaders of the mob, both of Middleport, were arrested and jailed, and their friends threatened to free them by force.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of A. G. Adams
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of A. G. Adams was a failed attempt, in late September 1882 at Bonanza, Colorado, to lynch the cashier of the Bonanza Exchange Bank after his arrest following the bank's suspension. According to the single dispatch that reported it, the lynching was prevented by "some law-abiding citizens," and Adams was not reported harmed.

episodes.title: Arnaudville night raid on Narcisse Semain's cabin
episodes.lead: The Arnaudville night raid on Narcisse Semain's cabin took place in September 1882, when an armed party of white men went at night to the home of Semain, a Black man living near Arnaudville, Louisiana, after a quarrel in the town. Semain shot and killed Marcellus Guitrot, a member of the party, and escaped. Local papers then disputed whether the men had come to punish him or as a constable's posse, and four of them were arrested on Semain's own affidavit.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bob Harris
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Bob Harris took place in Des Moines, Iowa, on the night of September 16, 1882, when a crowd of several hundred to perhaps 1,500 men rushed the county jail to hang a prisoner accused of beating and robbing the grocer John B. James. Sheriff Littleton had already sent Harris out of the city, and the crowd searched the jail, the courthouse and the state arsenal without finding him. Papers across the country carried the story as a frustrated case of "lynch law", and in December Harris was convicted and sentenced to the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Cook
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Charles Cook took place at Columbus, Indiana, on the night of September 20, 1882, when a band of masked men went after Cook, whom the dispatch called "a notorious wife beater," with the object of lynching him. Cook escaped, and the episode reached the press only as a one-sentence telegraphic item; none of the reports gives his race.

episodes.title: Killing of Crockett Jenkins
episodes.lead: The killing of Crockett Jenkins was the hanging of a man described as a member of the Campbell gang, whose body was found on a hilltop oak near Princeton in Caldwell County, Kentucky, in late September 1882. One Kentucky paper called it another hanging by a mob, but the fuller accounts said suspicion fell on Mary Sullivan and female relatives, who were arrested and released. The case drew attention chiefly because Mary Sullivan was herself hanged by a mob from the same limb about a week later.

episodes.title: Lancaster riot of 1882
episodes.lead: The Lancaster riot of 1882 was a shooting on 27 September 1882 in the main street of Lancaster, South Carolina, in which armed white men killed at least four Black men from a mounted procession after a political meeting addressed by the Independent congressional candidate E. B. C. Cash. Reported deaths rose from four to as many as twelve, while no white man was said to have been seriously hurt. Southern Democratic papers called the shooting self-defense against a drunken mob, whereas Northern Republican voices called it a massacre and political murder.

episodes.title: Killing of Dolly Durand
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of Dolly Durand was the shooting of a state's witness in a Texas murder trial by unidentified men as he slept outdoors near the Ingle settlement, reported from San Antonio, on the night of Saturday, September 30, 1882. No one was reported arrested, and the papers treated the killing as revenge for his testimony against John Lyons, whom a San Antonio jury had just acquitted.

episodes.title: Helena election-day violence (1882)
episodes.lead: The Helena election-day violence took place at the Phillips County courthouse in Helena, Arkansas, on September 4, 1882, when Democrats and deputy sheriffs beat Republican ticket distributors and drove a crowd of about 1,000 Black voters from the polls. A deputy sheriff fired three times at a Black man, few Black men voted, and the Democrats claimed the county. Republican papers across the North treated the episode as the worst case of "bulldozing" in the state election, while Democratic papers dismissed it as invention.

episodes.title: Shooting of a fleeing prisoner in Maysville, Kentucky (1882)
episodes.lead: The shooting of a fleeing prisoner in Maysville, Kentucky, took place on the night of September 19, 1882, when special policeman Fred. Bodie shot a Black man who had broken away from him after an arrest for obstructing the sidewalk. The man, whose name was not printed, was wounded in the hip, an injury the local paper described as slight.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Allen
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Frank Allen took place in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on the night of September 6, 1882, when a mob fought police officers in an effort to lynch Allen after he was accused of shooting two men in a saloon. The officers secured Allen and he was locked up; the mob's attempt is known from a single wire dispatch, and no report gives the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Lynching of Gus Knight
episodes.lead: The lynching of Gus Knight was the killing of a Black man by a mob near Bartow, Jefferson County, Georgia, on September 11, 1882. Knight, accused of assaulting a married white woman that morning, was taken from two constables and shot. Georgia papers presented the killing as deserved vengeance, and a short wire telegram carried it to papers across the South and Midwest.

episodes.title: Rape of Henrietta Robinson
episodes.lead: The rape of Henrietta Robinson was an assault on a Black woman by three white men, Maurice Connors, Patrick McNulty and James Reynolds, in the Swampoodle district of northeast Washington, D.C., in the early hours of September 3, 1882. Police arrested all three that night, and in November a jury convicted Connors of rape and found the other two guilty as accessories, a verdict the judge then set aside. The Washington dailies followed the case for nearly four months, and one paper's first headline said it was a case where "Judge Lynch" should have a say.

episodes.title: False report of the lynching of J. J. Bowles
episodes.lead: The false report of the lynching of J. J. Bowles was a story, printed in Montana Territory newspapers in September 1882, that cowboys had hanged Bowles, a Judith Basin saloon keeper, near Fort Maginnis for setting a prairie fire. The story was reprinted as far away as Omaha, Cheyenne and Savannah before Bowles himself wrote in October that it was a lie. The Fort Benton River Press, which first published it, admitted in November that it had been wrong.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching in Gonzales County, Texas (1882)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching in Gonzales County, Texas, was the pursuit in late September 1882 of an unnamed Black prisoner, charged with assaulting a 12-year-old girl near Gonzales, by a mob reported at about 250 men. Officers moved him from jail to jail and finally by night and rail to San Antonio, where he was lodged safely in jail. The Dallas Herald told the story as a 'thrilling game of hide-and-seek' won by a state Ranger, Sergeant Rudd.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Hunter
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Hunter was a failed attack by a masked mob on the jail at Washington, Daviess County, Indiana, in the night of September 9-10, 1882, to seize and lynch Hunter, who was held for the killing of William Lentz. An armed guard placed by the sheriff held the jail, and the mob dispersed after appeals from the sheriff and the prosecuting attorney. The story ran as a telegraphic brief across the country, and Hunter was later convicted at Vincennes and sentenced to hang.

episodes.title: Killing of John Spicy
episodes.lead: The killing of John Spicy was the fatal shooting of a Black man, also named in the papers as Lucius Edmunds, by men sent to arrest him at or near Leary's, Georgia, in late September 1882. The telegraphic dispatch from Atlanta described a fight with a sheriff's posse in which Spicy wounded one of the posse and accidentally shot his wife before he was killed. The brief dispatch ran in papers from Washington to Seattle, while a later Georgia account gave a different, longer sequence of events.

episodes.title: Rising Fawn marshal shooting
episodes.lead: The Rising Fawn marshal shooting was the killing of an unnamed Black man by Marshal J. M. Surry at Rising Fawn on the morning of September 29, 1882. According to the only account, a special telegraphed from Decatur, Alabama, the man tried to shoot the marshal as he was about to be arrested, and the marshal shot him dead. The story reached papers across the West as a one-sentence wire item.

episodes.title: Lynching of Nathan Bonnet
episodes.lead: The lynching of Nathan Bonnet took place at Williston, South Carolina, on the night of Wednesday, September 13, 1882, when a body of lynchers overpowered the jailer, took Bonnet, a Black prisoner, from the town jail, hanged him and riddled his body with bullets. Bonnet, described as seventeen years old, had been accused of entering a white man's house at midnight and attempting to rape his daughter, and was said to have confessed in jail. A short wire dispatch carried the story across the country within days, often under headlines approving the killing, while a South Carolina paper published a fuller account that praised it.

episodes.title: Killing of George Hathaway
episodes.lead: The killing of George Hathaway was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a white man, Martin Murphy, at a Black dance in Carlisle, Kentucky, on the night of September 27, 1882. Hathaway died on October 2, and Murphy escaped while armed men searched for him. A national wire brief retold the case as a white man defying a ban on white dancers, and it circulated from Delaware to Montana.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Pat Carmody
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Pat Carmody was a Saturday-night armed attack, most likely on September 23, 1882, on the house of P. (Pat) Carmody near San Marcial, New Mexico Territory, by people who suspected him of leading the mob that had hanged Wm. Wiggins the night before. Carmody held his fortified house through an exchange of some two hundred shots and later took refuge with soldiers at Fort Craig.

episodes.title: Lynching near Comanche, Texas (September 1882)
episodes.lead: The lynching near Comanche, Texas, was the killing in September 1882 of an unnamed Black man accused of raping a white girl, whom a posse pursued for ten miles, captured and lynched. The episode is known only from one-sentence telegraphic briefs that ran in papers from Tennessee to Dakota over the following two weeks.

episodes.title: Dubuque jail attack on two Black roustabouts
episodes.lead: The Dubuque jail attack on two Black roustabouts was a beating of two Black prisoners by white fellow inmates in the jail at Dubuque, Iowa, in late summer 1882. The two men were struck with chair-rounds and table-legs until court-house officers stopped what the papers called a riot. Papers outside Iowa ran the item as an example of race prejudice in the North, describing it as 'an effort to draw the color line'.

episodes.title: East St. Louis school dispute of 1882
episodes.lead: The East St. Louis school dispute of 1882 was a conflict in East St. Louis, Illinois, in September 1882, when Black children refused a separate school site were turned away from the white schools and street fights followed. The schools were closed on two successive days, and fights between white and Black children were reported before the dispute was said to have ended on September 13 with Black families accepting separate schools. Wire versions ran nationally under headlines such as "A War of Races" and "The Color Line."

episodes.title: Chattanooga jail mob of September 1882
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Chattanooga jail mob of September 1882 was a gathering of a crowd reported at 5,000 around the jail at Chattanooga, Tennessee, on the night of September 18, 1882, demanding the Taylor brothers, who were wanted for killing the Hamilton County sheriff and his deputy. The brothers had not in fact been captured, and after a committee from the crowd searched the jail and found them absent, the crowd dispersed without harming anyone. Wire reports noted that leading citizens took part, and dispatches the next day labeled the crowd "Disappointed Lynchers."

episodes.title: Killing of Thomas Phearby
episodes.lead: The killing of Thomas Phearby took place on September 1, 1882, when Officer John Foster shot Phearby, a Black prisoner in his charge, in the woods about four miles from Spartanburg, South Carolina. A coroner's jury found that Phearby died from a pistol ball fired by Foster, and Foster was jailed.

episodes.title: Hanging of William Wiggins
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The hanging of William Wiggins was the killing of an old man at San Marcial, New Mexico Territory, about September 22, 1882, by men who took him from his house and hanged him over its door. A Socorro correspondent called it 'cold blooded murder' and said Wiggins was killed because he was the main witness in a peonage case. Soon afterward a crowd blamed a local man, P. Carmody, and tried without success to lynch him.

episodes.title: Lynching of Winston Wade
episodes.lead: The lynching of Winston Wade took place at Union City, Tennessee, on the night of September 5, 1882, when a mob of about one hundred men took Wade, a Black man, from custody and hanged him to the limb of a tree. Wade had been accused of outraging Mrs. Sarah J. Young, a white woman, near the town three days earlier. A Nashville dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and several papers printed it under headlines approving the hanging.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Beaner
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Beaner was a night ride by a party of horsemen on the Loudoun County jail at Leesburg, Virginia, on 7 September 1882, aimed at seizing and lynching a Black youth held there. The riders reached the jail, met the jailor and his sons, and turned back without trying to enter, and Beaner was not harmed. Local papers treated the failed raid with derision or, in one case, regret that the sheriff had been ready.

episodes.title: Lynching of J. A. Archuleta
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of J. A. Archuleta took place on the night of Sunday, October 29, 1882, when a crowd of Mexicans took Archuleta, a justice of the peace and banker of Conejos, Colorado, from custody in northwestern New Mexico and lynched him. He was accused of shooting and killing Deputy Sheriff Blancett a few days earlier. Papers across the country carried the news chiefly because the dead man was a judge and 'prominent banker and merchant'.

episodes.title: Tarring and feathering of Andrew Elliott
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The tarring and feathering of Andrew Elliott was a night attack at Grand Forks, Dakota Territory, in late October 1882, in which a 'vigilance committee' seized a man accused of exposing himself to school girls, threatened to hang him, and covered him with tar and feathers. Elliott survived, and within days Grand Forks dispatches reported that townspeople doubted his guilt and called the affair an outrage.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Antonio de Ritta
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Antonio de Ritta took place in St. Louis, Missouri, on the evening of October 26, 1882, when a crowd of Italian neighbors seized de Ritta, a Sicilian rag-picker, after a 7-year-old boy was shot dead in the yard of their Almond Street row. A police officer got him away from the crowd by locking him inside a street alarm box until a patrol wagon arrived, and a coroner's jury later held him for the boy's murder.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Robert Wilson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Robert Wilson took place in Memphis, Tennessee, in the early hours of October 2, 1882, when a crowd of about 200 to 250 people gathered at the Shelby County jail and demanded Wilson, a 19-year-old Black prisoner accused of fatally shooting a grocer. The jailer refused to give up the keys and the crowd dispersed, and Wilson was later convicted of murder and sentenced to hang. Wire reports carried the story nationally as a failed lynching by a crowd that lacked a leader, while a Memphis daily openly regretted the failure.

episodes.title: Mock hanging of an accused burglar at Nebraska City
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The mock hanging of an accused burglar at Nebraska City was an episode in October 1882 in which a party of Nebraska City 'lynchers' repeatedly hanged and revived a man accused of burglary. The man survived and, given the choice between a final hanging and leaving the country, he left. A Connecticut weekly carried the story as an oddity because the lynchers had 'varied the usual course of proceedings'.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Thurber
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Thurber took place on October 24, 1882, at Grand Forks, Dakota Territory, when a crowd broke into the county jail, took Thurber, a Black barber, from the sheriff, and hanged him from the railroad bridge. Thurber had been accused the day before of assaulting a fifteen-year-old girl and Mrs. Samuel Burbank, the wife of a railroad conductor, near Norton. The papers dwelt on the fight with the officers and the husband's part in the hanging, and several editors defended it.

episodes.title: Killing of Daniel King at Kenner, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The killing of Daniel King was the fatal shooting of a drummer-boy at Kenner, Louisiana, on a Saturday evening in early October 1882, during the fall election season. The two surviving accounts disagree on who he was: a Mississippi weekly described a Black Democrat boy shot by a crowd of Black Republicans, while a wire brief called him a white drummer-boy killed in a political riot.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Emil Peppercorn
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Emil Peppercorn took place on October 23, 1882, when crowds at Calhoun and Blair, in Washington County, Nebraska, threatened a German music teacher being brought back from St. Louis to stand trial for eloping with a 14-year-old pupil. Sheriff Gross got him into the Blair jail ahead of the crowd, and no report says he was harmed.

episodes.title: Lynching of J. H. Capps
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of J. H. Capps took place at Fort Fetterman, Albany County, Wyoming Territory, on the night of October 12, 1882, when a party of masked men took the cowboy from the post guard house and hanged him. Capps had been accused of shooting dead Richard P. Elgin, a bookkeeper for the cattle firm of Searight Bros., earlier that afternoon. Wyoming papers openly approved the hanging, and wire reports carried it nationally as the second lynching in the county within a short time.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George H. Tew
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of George H. Tew took place on October 12, 1882, at the Aquidneck Park fair near Newport, Rhode Island, when a crowd tried to lynch Tew, a young special officer, after he struck a boy with his club. Tew escaped to a neighboring farmhouse, where regular officers protected him, and the next day he was charged with beating the boy. Papers across the country carried the story as a near-lynching of a policeman, and most of them blamed the officer.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Holloway
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Holloway took place on Tuesday, October 3, 1882, when a crowd seized Holloway, a young Black man accused of raping a white woman, at the end of a magistrates' hearing at Elkton in Giles County, Tennessee, and hanged him from the iron bridge over the Elk River.
