A short wire dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and Tennessee papers openly approved the killing.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Lempke
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Henry Lempke was a failed attempt by residents of St. Peter, Minnesota, to hang a cigar-factory worker accused on October 13, 1882, of attempting to rape a three-year-old girl. Lempke was held in jail, tried a month later and sentenced to two and a half years in the penitentiary, a term several Minnesota papers called too light.

episodes.title: Lynching of Hume Redman
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Hume Redman took place in Evansville, Indiana, early on October 11, 1882, when about 100 armed men from Posey County broke into the county jail, took out Redman, who was accused of killing his wife, and killed him in the street. Police fired on the retreating mob, and one of its members, David Murphy, was also killed. Papers across the country carried the story as a street battle between officers and lynchers, and several editors defended the killing of Redman.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Rhodes
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jim Rhodes took place in the early morning of October 2, 1882, when masked, armed men took him from the jail at Charlottesville, Virginia, and hanged him from an oak tree on the Free Bridge road. Rhodes was awaiting trial for the axe murders of John O. Massie and his wife, an elderly Albemarle County couple, and the lynchers held off the commonwealth's attorney at gunpoint. Virginia papers disputed whether his last words were a confession and whether the jail's guards had been overpowered.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Brooks
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Brooks took place at Jacksonville, Alabama, on October 5, 1882, when a large crowd took Brooks, a Black prisoner, from the sheriff after his preliminary hearing and hanged him on the outskirts of the town. Brooks had been accused of assaulting a little girl near Anniston, and a wire dispatch from Anniston carried the story to dailies across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Watson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Watson took place about October 27, 1882, when railroad laborers on the Oregon Short Line hanged him at the Kelton road crossing, about ten miles below Patton's station, after an improvised trial. Watson was accused of shooting and robbing a fellow laborer, William Fox, and his alleged accomplice, Cash Austin, was handed to a deputy sheriff and later freed. A wire story three weeks later carried the case to eastern papers, placing it at "Pattersons Station" with a Yankton, Dakota dateline.

episodes.title: Lynching of Johnson and "Tex" at American Falls
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Johnson and "Tex" took place at American Falls, Idaho Territory, on the night of Sunday, 8 October 1882, when townsmen hanged two men they suspected of murdering a Chinese man from the Oregon Short Line Railroad bridge over the Snake river. The hanging followed an order to leave town and a gunfight with the citizens and the night watchman. An Ogden account carried the story through Idaho, Utah, Nevada, California and Montana papers, and no report gives the race of either man.

episodes.title: Shooting of Louis Guilford
episodes.lead: The shooting of Louis Guilford took place at Tarboro, North Carolina, on October 23, 1882, when Guilford, a Black man under arrest, was shot and mortally wounded by men who pursued and recaptured him after he escaped. According to the dispatch, Guilford had cut the arresting constable with a razor and wounded two of his captors, and papers across the country ran the story as the act of a "fighting" or "murderous" Black man.

episodes.title: Lynching of Mary Sullivan
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Mary Sullivan was the hanging of a woman by a mob of about fifty men in Caldwell County, Kentucky, in early October 1882, after she was taken at night from a house near Dalton in neighboring Hopkins County. She had been accused of a part in the hanging of Crockett Jenkins, a member of the Campbell gang, and released, and no clue to her killers was reported. Papers across the country retold her story as that of a "female desperado," while two Kentucky papers objected to the mob hanging of a woman.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Riley Anderson (October 1882)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Riley Anderson was a night raid on the Greenville County jail in Greenville, South Carolina, on October 2, 1882, by a party of white and Black men seeking to hang Anderson, a Black man accused of murdering a woman and her infant. Warned in advance, Sheriff Gilreath had already hidden Anderson, and the crowd dispersed after the sheriff spoke to it. South Carolina papers carried the story chiefly from the Greenville News, dwelling on the sheriff's stratagem.

episodes.title: Killing of Sid Dixon
episodes.lead: The killing of Sid Dixon was the fatal shooting of a Black mill hand by armed white pursuers in western Fulton County, Kentucky, near Hickman, in October 1882. After a week of quarrels, whites calling themselves a sheriff's posse hunted Dixon and other Black men; one report said Dixon was shot dead and two others wounded, while the local paper reported only wounds.

episodes.title: Lynching of Andrew Jackson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Andrew Jackson was the killing of a Black man by a mob in early November 1882, reported as having taken place near Vienna, in Lincoln Parish, Louisiana. Jackson was accused of assaulting a white girl, whom one report described as eight years old. The killing reached national readers only as a one-sentence item, first under a Vicksburg, Mississippi, dateline and then in weekly news-brief columns.

episodes.title: Death of William Berg at Breckenridge, Minnesota
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The death of William Berg at Breckenridge, Minnesota, occurred about November 20, 1882, when Berg, who had just shot William Little in a drunken row, drowned in the river while fleeing. Little died days later on a train taking him home to Dubuque. One Montana paper reported that a crowd had rushed Berg intending to lynch him and was cheated of him by his drowning, a detail absent from the Minnesota accounts.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bill Harris
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bill Harris was the shooting of a Black man by a pursuing mob at his wife's house in Bastrop parish, Louisiana, around November 1, 1882. Harris was accused of attacking the young daughter of a white planter named Wilder, and the party that captured him fired twenty guns at him at once. The story reached papers across the country through a Shreveport wire dispatch under headlines such as "Twenty Shots at One Man."

episodes.title: Lynching of an alleged cattle thief near Coleman, Texas (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of an alleged cattle thief near Coleman, Texas, was the hanging in late November 1882 of an unnamed man described as one of a gang charged with stealing cattle near Comanche. It was one of several hangings of the alleged gang's members within about a week, which Texas and wire reports said broke the gang up. No report gives the man's name, his race, or who hanged him.

episodes.title: Whipping of Bibb County chain gang convicts
episodes.lead: The whipping of Bibb County chain gang convicts was the beating of two Black convicts by a guard of the county chain gang in Bibb County, Georgia, reported in November 1882. The Bibb County grand jury proposed to investigate the case, and within days the county's Road Commissioners gave up control of the chain gang to the County Commissioners.

episodes.title: Florence election riot (1882)
episodes.lead: The Florence election riot was an attack on Black voters at the polls at or near Florence, South Carolina, on election day, November 7, 1882, in which two or three "colored men" were shot and the election there was broken up. The news came chiefly from a telegram by E. H. Deas, the Republican candidate for Congress in the Sixth District, who said the men were shot for insisting on voting the Republican ticket. Wire reports turned his account into two or three killed, and Republican papers in the North cited it as an example of Democratic intimidation.

episodes.title: Shooting of Hicks by Constable King
episodes.lead: The shooting of Hicks by Constable King took place in Sampson County, North Carolina, in late November 1882, when a constable serving an arrest warrant seriously wounded Hicks, a Black schoolteacher. The only surviving report, a brief item from the Clinton Caucasian reprinted in Raleigh, said that Hicks had resisted the officer with an axe.

episodes.title: Killing of Israel Groff
episodes.lead: The killing of Israel Groff took place on November 7, 1882, election day, when Frederick, Maryland, policeman Porter shot Groff, a Black man, dead during a fight at a city polling precinct. A crowd that the National Republican put at several hundred Black men then surrounded the house of Judge John A. Lynch, where the officer had taken refuge, and threatened to lynch him before he was taken to jail. Porter was released on bail eleven days later, and accounts of why he fired differed sharply.

episodes.title: Killing of Jack Hendricks
episodes.lead: The killing of Jack Hendricks was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Constable Wright in Campbell County, Virginia, near Lynchburg, on November 9, 1882. Hendricks was under arrest for "malicious cutting," and the only published account, a brief Lynchburg dispatch, said he was shot while trying to escape. The dispatch ran the next day in papers from Richmond to Dallas and St. Paul, usually as a single line among other news.

episodes.title: Ashland mob attack on the Granite State (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Ashland mob attack on the Granite State took place on November 1, 1882, when a mob at Ashland, Kentucky, tried to seize William Neal and Ellis Craft, prisoners accused of murder, from State Guard troops carrying them down the Ohio River. The troops fired on the mob's ferryboat and on the crowd watching from the bank, killing five or six townspeople, while the prisoners reached jail unharmed. A coroner's jury held the troops' commander culpable for the killings.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joseph Stout
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Joseph Stout was a threatened mob hanging in Montgomery County, Indiana, on the night of November 25, 1882, when mobs gathered at Colfax and Darlington to seize Stout as officers took him by train to the Crawfordsville jail. Stout had been arrested in Indianapolis that day, accused of murdering and robbing a Darlington grocer, Taylor Dunbar. The officers left the train early and drove to Crawfordsville, where Stout was jailed unharmed, and wire reports carried the story under headlines about his narrow escape.

episodes.title: Killing of Julius Hurt
episodes.lead: The killing of Julius Hurt was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a local officer, William Jones, at Campbellsville, Kentucky, on November 27, 1882. Jones said Hurt had resisted arrest on a bench warrant, and he was acquitted at an examining trial the same day. A short dispatch about the killing ran in papers from Washington to California, one of which counted it as Kentucky's "daily murder."

episodes.title: Wilmington Third Ward election riot
episodes.lead: The Wilmington Third Ward election riot was a fight between a white crowd and a party of Black men near the Third Ward polls in Wilmington, Delaware, on the afternoon of election day, November 7, 1882. Several men in the crowd were shot, a Black man named Lewis Woodland had his skull fractured by a stone, and three Black men were later charged with riot. The local Republican paper said the whites began the fight, while the Associated Press dispatch printed across the country called the Black men the assailants.

episodes.title: Lynching of a Mexican man near Loma Parda, New Mexico
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of a Mexican man near Loma Parda, New Mexico, took place on November 13, 1882, when he was hanged for the alleged murder of a Fort Union soldier of the 23rd infantry. Accounts differ on whether soldiers or 'unknown parties' hanged him, and a later western-news brief said he had been proved innocent.

episodes.title: Lynching of David N. Lee
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of David N. Lee was the hanging of a young man by unknown parties on the Brake road near Holly Grove Church in Franklin Parish, Louisiana, in late 1882. A card left in his pocket blamed "hog meat," and the Lake Charles Echo reported that a mob had hanged him on mere suspicion of stealing hogs. The governor offered a reward for each member of the mob, and both papers that reported the killing condemned it.

episodes.title: Rockingham registration fight (1882)
episodes.lead: The Rockingham registration fight was an attack by a large party of white men on a revenue officer named Spears and about 100 Black men he had brought to register as voters at Rockingham, North Carolina, on election day, November 7, 1882. Spears was badly beaten and several of the Black men were severely injured, and many arrests were reported.

episodes.title: Lynching of Counce O'Neal
episodes.lead: The lynching of Counce O'Neal was the killing of a Black man near Dublin, Georgia, in late November 1882, when a group of men took him from his house at night and riddled his body with bullets. A Macon dispatch said he had been killed for an alleged assault on a little girl and was afterward found to be innocent, while other reports blamed Black neighbors with a grudge.

episodes.title: Setauket rubber factory riot
episodes.lead: The Setauket rubber factory riot was an attack in late October or early November 1882 by Irish and other white residents of Setauket, Long Island, New York, on the town's Black residents, who, like the Irish, had recently come there in large numbers to work in the rubber factory. After a white man was reported beaten by Black men, whites beat every Black man they found on the streets and attacked Black homes until armed Black residents drove them off. No deaths were reported, and the story ran nationally as a race feud under headings such as "An Irish-African Feud" and "A War of Races."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Smith (Ogden, 1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Frank Smith took place in Ogden, Utah Territory, on the night of Saturday, 18 November 1882, when a party of men set out to lynch Smith, who was held in custody, accused of shooting a railroad brakeman, Patsy Jones. The men could not find the place where Smith was confined and disbanded; Jones later died, and Smith was reported held in the Penitentiary. No report gives the race of Smith or of Jones.

episodes.title: Nashville streetcar riot (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Nashville streetcar riot took place on the night of November 6, 1882, when a Black crowd at a Republican rally on Cherry street in Nashville, Tennessee, seized the driver of a streetcar that had run over and killed an elderly Black man, Alfred King, and tried to lynch him. Police and a constable got the wounded driver, Benjamin Woodward, to jail, which citizens and soldiers then guarded against the crowd.

episodes.title: Vienna, Louisiana, jail lynching (1882)
episodes.lead: The Vienna, Louisiana, jail lynching took place on the night of November 6, 1882, when a group of men forced the jail at Vienna and took out four Black prisoners who had been sent there from Jackson parish for safekeeping. Two of the prisoners, charged with robbing and trying to kill an elderly white man named Ray, were found the next morning shot to death outside town, while one escaped and another was reportedly spared. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and Louisiana papers followed with their own notices.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Keller and William Coulter
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Keller and William Coulter took place on the night of Saturday, 18 November 1882, when a mob surrounded the jail at Taylorville, Christian County, Illinois, where the two men were held. The men had been arrested for the alleged criminal assault of a 16-year-old girl at Pana, and the mob had not taken them at last report. Papers outside the state tied the case to other Christian County crimes, and two predicted a lynching to come.

episodes.title: Manhunt and shooting of Wesley Fisher
episodes.lead: The manhunt and shooting of Wesley Fisher took place near Cumberland, Maryland, in late October and early November 1882, when Fisher, a young Black man accused of raping a farmer's wife, was hunted by armed citizens and shot by two private captors on November 3. He survived his wounds and was jailed amid threats of lynching, which the sheriff was reported determined to resist. Fisher denied the charge, was identified by the woman at a hearing, and was held for the grand jury.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unnamed Black man near Millen, Georgia (1882)
episodes.lead: The lynching of an unnamed Black man near Millen, Georgia, took place in December 1882, when a mob overpowered the posse taking him to jail and killed him. He had been accused of attempting to assault a young white woman and had been bound over for trial. A Waynesboro letter in the Savannah Morning News and an Augusta wire dispatch reported the killing, and the wire carried it to papers across the country under headings such as "Lynch Law in Georgia."

episodes.title: Oconee Christmas Day riot
episodes.lead: The Oconee Christmas Day riot was an armed clash on December 25, 1882, at Oconee, Georgia, between the town marshal, the mayor and white citizens and a group of Black men the marshal was trying to arrest. Three or four Black men were shot, one reportedly mortally, and the marshal and his son were wounded. A Macon wire sent across the country on December 30 called it a "race riot" that had killed a white man, but a second Macon dispatch the same day said no one had been killed.

episodes.title: Killing of Bill Allen
episodes.lead: The killing of Bill Allen was the shooting by Chicago police of a Black waiter in a chicken coop near the North Halsted Street rail yards on Sunday afternoon, December 3, 1882, after a city-wide manhunt. Allen was accused of killing Officer Clarence E. Wright four days earlier, and the most widely printed dispatch said police shot him after he threw up his hands and offered to surrender. A crowd of thousands then tried to hang his body, and a coroner's jury exonerated the two officers who shot him.

episodes.title: Killing of Charles Smith (Waxahachie, 1882)
episodes.lead: The killing of Charles Smith was the shooting of a Black man by a posse of armed citizens at Waxahachie, Texas, in December 1882, shortly after he was said to have shot and killed City Marshal J. H. Spalding, who was trying to arrest him. Cornered in a privy about an hour after the marshal's death, Smith was 'riddled with bullets', and a coroner's jury attributed his death to unknown parties summoned by the sheriff. The story circulated nationally as a brief wire item in which the marshal's 'murderer' met a swift end.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charley Branch
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charley Branch took place late on the night of Tuesday, December 26, 1882, near Varner Station, Arkansas, when an armed mob took Branch, a Black man, from his guards and hanged him to a telegraph pole. Branch had been arrested two days earlier, accused of ravishing and murdering a nine-year-old girl. A short Little Rock wire dispatch carried the news across the country, and several papers headlined it with approval, the Omaha Daily Bee calling it "A Deed to Applaud."

episodes.title: Atlanta Christmas police shooting (1882)
episodes.lead: The Atlanta Christmas police shooting was the wounding of an unnamed Black man by an Atlanta policeman, who shot him in the leg on Christmas Day, 1882. The only reason given was that the man had tried to take the officer's club, and the shooting reached northern papers as one line in a wire list of Atlanta's Christmas "casualties."

episodes.title: Lynching of Dick the Diver
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dick the Diver was the killing of a man known only by that nickname by a crowd of vigilantes at Weeksville, a Northern Pacific Railroad construction camp in Missoula County, Montana Territory, on the evening of December 5, 1882. Accused of robbery, he was shot and, by most Montana accounts, hanged by a crowd of seventy or eighty citizens acting on a mass meeting's vow to clear the town of desperadoes. Papers in Montana, the Dakotas, Nevada and Washington treated it as a sign of the lawlessness of the camp, and none gave the victim's real name or race.

episodes.title: Shooting of Hannibal Lee
episodes.lead: The shooting of Hannibal Lee was the wounding of a Black man by Town Marshal Jim Walker in Pineville, Louisiana, on Saturday, December 2, 1882. Lee was reported "dangerously wounded," and the only surviving report justified the shooting by saying he had resisted arrest and assaulted the marshal.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Forman
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Henry Forman was a gathering of a crowd at the jail in Helena, Montana Territory, on the night of December 22, 1882, aimed at hanging Forman, who was being held for shooting his son-in-law, Jacob Kenck. The crowd was persuaded to disperse, and Forman was later remanded to await the grand jury.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Herndon
episodes.lead: The killing of Henry Herndon was the fatal shooting of a Black man, described as "colored," by James Dameron, a policeman, at Springfield, Missouri, in late 1882. It is known only from a one-line item in a Kentucky paper's news column, which attributed the shooting to "an old grudge."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ben Rushing at James Bayou, Missouri
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ben Rushing took place at James Bayou, Missouri, after Rushing was accused of shooting J. B. Lindsey dead there on Christmas Day, December 25, 1882. A wire dispatch from Cairo, Illinois, reported that the accused man was in the hands of a mob and that lynching was expected, but the Cairo Bulletin later reported that he had been captured and jailed at Charleston, Missouri. No report gives the race of either man.

episodes.title: Lynching of George W. and Jim Fraley
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of George W. and Jim Fraley was the hanging of two brothers by an armed mob near Hazel Dell, Comanche County, Texas, in late 1882, after they had been arrested on a charge of stealing cotton. The mob took the brothers from their guard at night and hanged them from the same limb of a tree. Wire dispatches from Dallas carried the story to papers across the country, several of which stressed that the younger brother was 'a mere boy.'

episodes.title: Killing of Gray in Hawkins County, Tennessee
episodes.lead: The killing of Gray took place in December 1882 in the mountainous part of Hawkins County, Tennessee, when a party of white men came to his cabin at night to whip him over an accusation that he had stolen hogs. In the gunfire that followed, Gray, a Black man, was mortally wounded and died, his stepson's thigh was broken, and two of the white men were wounded. A Knoxville dispatch describing it as a "terrible tragedy" ran in papers across the country.

episodes.title: Killing of Joe Ross
episodes.lead: The killing of Joe Ross was the fatal shooting of Joe Ross, a Black man also known as Joe Wilson, by ferryman Alonzo Huntley at Ivy's Mill on the Catawba River in Lancaster County, South Carolina, on the night of December 6, 1882. Ross was being hunted by a party of Camden citizens as the accused killer of F. N. McDowell, and they had posted the ferryman at the crossing. Wire services carried the news across the country, and North Carolina papers hailed it as revenge for two killings Ross was said to have confessed.

episodes.title: Killing of Joe Walker
episodes.lead: The killing of Joe Walker took place at Skipwith, Mississippi, on the night of Saturday, December 9, 1882, when constable J. A. Lawson shot Walker, a Black man, while trying to arrest him for gambling. Walker died of the wound two days later, and Lawson was arrested and released on bail. The only account, a dispatch from Skipwith giving the constable's side, ran as a short crime item in papers from Mississippi to Minnesota.

episodes.title: Killing of Joe Ross
episodes.lead: The killing of Joe Ross was the fatal shooting of a Black man, known in Camden, South Carolina, as Joe Wilson, by ferryman Alonzo Huntley at Ivey's Mill on the Catawba River in Lancaster County on the night of December 6, 1882. Ross was accused of killing F. M. McDowell, a white Camden man, with an axe on Thanksgiving morning, and he was shot while fleeing a citizens' party from Camden that was described as 'bent on lynching him' and that had posted the ferryman. He died the next morning after giving what the papers called a confession, and his death was reported by wire across the country.

episodes.title: Killing of John Franklin
episodes.lead: The killing of John Franklin was the fatal shooting of a Black prisoner by City Marshal John Way in a cell of the jail at South Charleston, Ohio, on the night of December 25, 1882. Way said Franklin attacked him when he entered the cell, and that account, from a single dispatch, was printed across the country among the season's 'Christmas crimes'.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Lebanon Cemetery body snatchers
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of the Lebanon Cemetery body snatchers took place in Philadelphia on December 5, 1882, when a crowd of Black residents outside a magistrate's office threatened to lynch four men charged with stealing bodies from a Black burial ground. Police held off two rushes and took the prisoners to the Central station, and the wire carried the story under headlines such as "The Ghouls Nearly Lynched."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Lockie at Thomson, Georgia
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Lockie at Thomson, Georgia, took place after John L. Cushion was shot and killed there on the night of December 10, 1882, and a Black man named Lockie was arrested on suspicion. According to an Augusta dispatch, "the people" were restrained "with great difficulty" from lynching him, and no killing of the accused was reported. The story ran as a one-sentence wire item in December 1882 and was carried into weekly news digests later that month.

episodes.title: Oconee riot of 1882
episodes.lead: The Oconee riot of 1882 was a gun and knife fight at Oconee, Georgia, on Christmas Day, Dec. 25, 1882, in which the town marshal, his son, the mayor and white citizens shot several Black men who resisted an arrest. Three or four Black men were wounded, one of them reported likely to die, and the marshal and his son were also hurt. Georgia and national papers called it a 'riot' and a 'race riot', but their counts of the dead and wounded differed widely.

episodes.title: Sedalia police shooting of 1882
episodes.lead: The Sedalia police shooting of 1882 was an incident in Sedalia, Missouri, probably on the afternoon of 4 December 1882, in which Officer Wentzelman clubbed an unnamed Black man he had arrested and then fired three pistol shots at him as he fled. None of the shots hit him, and the man escaped. The only known account is a short local item in the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo, told from the officer's side.

episodes.title: Lynching near Millen, Georgia (1882)
episodes.lead: The lynching near Millen, Georgia, was the killing in December 1882 of an unnamed Black man whom a mob took from the officers escorting him to jail. He had been arrested and bound over for trial on a charge of attempting to outrage a young white woman. An Augusta wire dispatch carried the case to papers across the country, where shortened copies misnamed the place as "Nelson" or "Wilton."

episodes.title: Lynching of Riley at Caddoa
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Riley at Caddoa was the killing of a man named Riley by twelve to fifteen armed men at the Santa Fe railroad station at Caddoa, reported as in New Mexico, one night in mid-December 1882. Accused of murdering a tank tender, he was taken from the emigrant train, shot as he ran, and hanged from a telegraph pole in front of the passengers. The Wichita City Eagle printed the fullest account and complained that the Associated Press had published nothing about it.

episodes.title: Lincolnton riot arrests and banishment (1882)
episodes.lead: The Lincolnton riot arrests and banishment took place in Lincolnton, North Carolina, in December 1882, when thirty Black men were jailed for a riot and, after trial, all but one were acquitted on condition that they leave the town. Wire reports of armed patrols, threats to burn the town and troops ordered to the scene spread nationally before dispatches from Charlotte and Lincolnton denied that any renewed trouble had occurred.

episodes.title: Prineville vigilante killings (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Prineville vigilante killings were the shooting of A. C. Swartz and the hanging of Sid Huston and Charles Luster by masked men at Prineville, Crook County, Oregon, on a night shortly before Christmas 1882. All three were accused of belonging to an organized band of horse thieves, and the killings were attributed to a vigilance committee of stockmen. Wire reports carried the story nationally as a lynching of desperate cowboys, while an Oregon paper condemned it as murder.

episodes.title: Hanging of Stafford's assailant at Columbus, Texas
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The hanging of Stafford's assailant at Columbus, Texas, was the killing of an unnamed man by friends of a son of Capt. Stafford on December 27, 1882, after the man was said to have shot young Stafford. The story survives only as a brief Galveston News special from Houston, reprinted in papers outside Texas among other crime news, and it gives neither the hanged man's name nor his race.

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas Kerr
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Thomas Kerr was the hanging of Thomas P. Kerr from a sycamore tree at the Pioneer mining camp in Arizona Territory early on December 26, 1882, by men of the camp who had tried him before their own jury of twelve. Kerr had been accused of shooting a man named as William Hartley or William Hartnett in a Pioneer saloon hours before. A Tucson Citizen dispatch carried the story across the country, and a coroner's jury later found that Kerr died by hanging by unknown parties.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Robinson and Bill Cephas
episodes.lead: The lynching of Tom Robinson and Bill Cephas took place at Bastrop, in Morehouse Parish, Louisiana, in early December 1882, when a body of men broke open the jail and hanged the two Black prisoners from a tree near the town. The two men were being held on a charge of shooting a young white man named Curry, who survived. The wire account, which said local opinion sided with the lynchers and blamed 'indulgent juries', ran in papers from Maine to California.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of W. S. Sims
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of W. S. Sims was a failed attempt by an armed band to take Sims, a white physician, from the Aiken County jail in Aiken, South Carolina, on the night of December 5, 1882. Militia ordered out by Governor Thompson guarded the jail, and the band of more than one hundred men turned back without attacking. The case drew notice because of the unnamed charge against Sims, and a week later he was moved to Columbia for safekeeping.

episodes.title: Covington lynching threat against Will Smith
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Covington lynching threat against Will Smith took place in Covington, Georgia, on the afternoon of December 23, 1882, when a large crowd met Sheriff Anderson bringing in Smith, who was accused of two shootings, and cried for him to be killed and hanged. The sheriff got Smith to jail through the crowd, and a strong guard was posted. Southern papers headed the story as a lynching threatened or in prospect, while short wires elsewhere reported only the killings.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unnamed prisoner at Starke, Florida
episodes.lead: The lynching of an unnamed prisoner at Starke, Florida, took place in Bradford County some time before early October 1882, when lynchers broke open the county jail and hanged a Black man held on a charge of assaulting a young woman. The only account is a short item in the Starke Weekly Telegraph, known from a reprint in the Savannah Morning News, and a Tallahassee editorial later listed the killing among Florida crimes whose perpetrators were still unpunished.

episodes.title: Shooting of Canless Blair
episodes.lead: The shooting of Canless Blair took place in or near Shelby, Cleveland County, North Carolina, in May 1882, when a sheriff's officer, B. F. Logan, wounded Blair, a Black man said to be an escaped convict, with rifle fire. A pistol shot that Blair was said to have fired at the officers struck George Wright, another Black man, in the leg. Blair survived and was jailed; the two papers that reported it told the officers' version.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Ferguson at Charleston, Massachusetts
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Ferguson at Charleston, Massachusetts, is known only from an editorial paragraph in the Benton Weekly Record of Benton, Montana, on June 29, 1882, which said that "Judge Lynch" had lately dealt with a man named Ferguson charged with outraging a widow and causing her death. The paragraph implied that Ferguson was killed but gave no date, description of the act, or race for anyone involved.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph from Raleigh County, West Virginia
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph was the beating and driving out of a Black schoolteacher by a mob in Raleigh County, West Virginia, reported in February 1882. According to Randolph's own statement, the mob beat him and ordered him to leave after a justice acquitted men he had had arrested, and he left to save his life. A Parkersburg paper headed its notice of the case "SHAMEFUL" while qualifying its comment on whether the statement was true.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Patrick Simpson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Patrick Simpson was a pair of mob threats in 1881 against a man from Fulton, New York, who had been brought to Richmond, Kentucky, under arrest after he was mistaken for a fugitive murderer named Rogers. A mob tried to lynch him when he arrived, and after a court discharged him a crowd surrounded the court-house; he escaped on foot and reached home about the start of 1882. Papers told it as a story of mistaken identity and a narrow escape, and none of them gave Simpson's race.

episodes.title: Lynching of Peter Corbin
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Peter Corbin was the reported killing of a prisoner taken from the Gilmer county jail at Ellijay, Georgia, by a party of masked men in early 1882. Corbin, charged with an outrage on a lady, was reported found the next day in woods near the town with his head severed from his body. The only account is a short item from the Dalton Citizen, which passed the story on as something it had learned and hoped was untrue.

episodes.title: Logan saloon murder lynching
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Logan saloon murder lynching was the killing by townsfolk of an unnamed man accused of murder in a drinking saloon at Logan, a Mormon settlement, at an unstated date before June 1882. It is known only from a single sentence in a June 1882 newspaper summary of a New York World correspondent's account of the town, which presented the lynching and the liquor ban that followed as part of the settlers' record of good order.
